## Overview

The final submission of your Final Project is due on Sunday, December 13^th^,
and is worth 15 points.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Dec 13^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: Submit your assignment by tagging `@kstarr791` and `@jelmerp`
  in a new Issue in your GitHub repo.

::: callout-tip
### Questions and advice

Don't hesitate to contact the instructors with questions about, for example:

- Specific expectations for the Final Project that are unclear to you
- Whether you are on the right track with adjustments we suggested
  after your progress report or presentation
- Advice on how to code or organize aspects of your project

We're happy to answer questions by email or during office hours.
:::

::: callout-warning
### Late submissions

Late submission may be accommodated depending on circumstances,
but to request it, you must contact both instructors by Wednesday, December 9^th^.
For late submissions without advance notice,
3 points will be subtracted for each day the submission is late.
:::

|                                      |        | -   Has informative and appropriate directory and file names                             |

|                                      |        |     that renders well on your GitHub repo's front page                                   |

|                                      |        | -   Has information for the instructors (or any other reader of the project!) about      |
|                                      |        |     where at OSC (within `PAS3493`) to find the raw data files, and other details        |
|                                      |        |     needed to rerun the analyses                                                         |
|                                      |        | -   With the above pieces of information, allows the instructors to successfully rerun   |
|                                      |        |     all scripts in your project                                                          |
|                                      |        | -   Uses containers (preferred) and/or OSC modules to run external software              |
|                                      |        |     (Conda environments are also fine). R packages can simply be installed as we did     |

+--------------------------------------+--------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

|                                      |        | -   Uses tools and commands that are (by and large) appropriate to accomplish its goals  |
|                                      |        | -   Includes both shell scripts and R scripts or Quarto documents                        |
|                                      |        | -   Uses extensive comments within scripts to document what is being done and why        |
|                                      |        | -   Uses no absolute paths in scripts (your protocol may contain some, for example to    |
|                                      |        |     point to the raw data)                                                               |
|                                      |        | -   Uses scripts that accept arguments where appropriate and minimize "hard-coding" of   |
|                                      |        |     potentially variable things like input/output dirs, file names, and some software    |
|                                      |        |     settings. Any hard-coded variables/constants that *are* present are clearly set at   |
|                                      |        |     the top of scripts.                                                                  |
|                                      |        | -   Has individual scripts that are not overly long and don't do multiple unrelated      |
|                                      |        |     things                                                                               |
|                                      |        | -   Has no or only clearly annotated lines that are "commented out" in scripts           |
|                                      |        | -   Uses shell scripts with proper `set` settings, and similar good practices as taught  |
|                                      |        |     in the course                                                                        |
+--------------------------------------+--------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Slurm batch jobs                     | 2      | -   Has one or more scripts that are run as Slurm batch jobs at OSC                      |
|                                      |        | -   Uses appropriate `sbatch` options                                                    |
|                                      |        | -   Appropriately manages Slurm log files                                                |
+--------------------------------------+--------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Version control                      | 2      | -   Has Git commit messages that are informative                                         |
|                                      |        | -   Has (at least reasonably) appropriate commits, e.g. individual Git commits don't     |
|                                      |        |     contain multiple completely unrelated edits                                          |
|                                      |        | -   Has a single `.gitignore` file to make Git ignore files like large raw data files,   |
|                                      |        |     and in most cases, results files                                                     |

## Detailed steps

The rubric above lists what we will look for.
Before you submit, we recommend that you take the following steps:

1. **Test whether your project can be rerun**, since we will try to do so when grading.
   Clone your GitHub repository into a new directory at OSC
   (e.g., `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/FP_test`),
   and follow your own protocol from the top,
   including rendering your Quarto document(s).
   This is a quick way to find files you forgot to commit,
   absolute paths, and steps missing from your protocol.
   You don't need to wait for long-running steps to finish:
   once a step has started successfully, you can cancel it with `scancel`.
   Afterwards, remove the test directory.

2. **Go through the rubric** item by item, and check your project against it.

3. **Describe your genAI use** in a short section of your README
   (or in your submission notes, see below):
   which genAI tools you used, and for what
   (for example, "Claude Code wrote a first draft of `scripts/trim.sh`,
   which I then edited", or "I didn't use genAI").
   A few sentences are enough.

4. **Optionally, add submission notes** for the instructors,
   either in a separate file (e.g., `doc/submission-notes.md`) or in a section of your README.
   For example, you may want to:
   - Give additional instructions for rerunning your project
   - Point out files in the repository that we should ignore
   - Indicate which files or parts of files were pre-existing
     (see the [general info page](FP-info.qmd#academic-integrity))

5. **Push your final version** to GitHub,
   and submit by tagging `@kstarr791` and `@jelmerp` in a new Issue in your repo.

Good luck!!
